claims.text: The feedstock is as-atomized AlCrFeNiSi powder with nominal composition and morphology typical of conventional laser additive manufacturing.
Elevating and controlling the build-platform temperature to 300–500°C during deposition is the proposed intervention.
Build-platform preheating reduces the thermal difference between the melt pool and surrounding material.
Reducing the melt-pool-to-surroundings temperature difference reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients lower residual thermal stresses during solidification.
Maintaining a moderately elevated platform temperature permits in situ stress relaxation.
Reduced thermal gradients produce a more uniform microstructure.
Reduced thermal gradients result in fewer heterogeneous grain boundaries.
Lower internal-stress accumulation diminishes cracking and porosity.
The moderated cooling rate caused by preheating promotes a more favorable phase distribution.
The moderated cooling rate caused by preheating promotes grain refinement.
The proposed phase distribution and grain refinement enhance mechanical strength.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will have lower residual stresses than components built on a cold substrate under otherwise conventional conditions.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will have improved tensile strength and ductility relative to cold-substrate builds.
Build-platform preheating will reduce processing complexity by reducing the need for post-build treatments.
Conventional cold-substrate laser additive manufacturing typically produces high residual stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and increased processing complexity.
The proposed intervention may not resolve stress-related problems in bulk components or geometries with extreme thermal gradients.
